Trajectory watch note: this is a dollar-equivalent bar that moves with the rupee — currently favorable to a USD earner (rupee has weakened, lowering the effective USD threshold) but reversible if the rupee strengthens; read as 'worsening' from the Indian government's own stated intent (fixing the bar in INR specifically to stop USD-favorable drift), not as a current hardship. MAJOR Citation-integrity fix (2026-08-25, [specialist]) — this fact had the threshold's own denomination backward, not just a stale conversion. As of a January 2025 Indian government revision (independently confirmed via terratern.com and forum-expat-management.com/Fragomen search snippets, both stating 'As of January 2025, India has revised its Employment Visa salary threshold to INR 16.25 lakhs per annum'), the Employment Visa income bar is fixed in RUPEES, not dollars — the government's own stated reason for the change was specifically to remove foreign-exchange fluctuation risk from what had previously been a USD-denominated rule. The prior version of this fact stated value_raw as '25000' (USD) with INR given as a rough derived approximation — exactly backward: INR 16,25,000 is now the actual fixed statutory figure, and any dollar equivalent is the ever-shifting approximation. At the current USD/INR rate (~95.9, 2026-08-25, cross-checked by search against multiple currency trackers), INR 16.25 lakh converts to approximately $16,950/year — a full ~32% below the previously-stated $25,000, because the rupee has weakened substantially since the ~65:1 rate implicit in that older $25,000 figure (a commonly-recycled historical conversion, not tied to any current rate). This directly answers the 2026-08-25 task's specific question (posed by [specialist]) of whether a clean INR-denominated hard-fail threshold exists for India: yes, this is that threshold, and its dollar-equivalent bar is real, currently moderate-to-substantial (~32% swing), and will keep moving with the exchange rate going forward — worth a fresh FX check whenever this fact is next touched, not treated as fixed. Tied to a single sponsoring employer; not applicable without a genuine qualifying Indian employer. Confidence held at Medium rather than raised, since the Jan-2025-revision claim itself rests on two aggregator sources (both 403'd on direct re-fetch this pass) rather than a directly-read MHA/PIB primary text — a real, named gap, not a confirmed primary-institutional citation.

fact_label: Employment (E) Visa converts to permanent residency
value_raw: No
notes: No time-based or status-based conversion exists from the Employment Visa (or any work/business visa) to permanent residency (PR). India's only PR-adjacent mechanism, the Permanent Residency Status (PRS) scheme (Ministry of Home Affairs, launched 31 Aug 2016), is a wholly separate track gated on foreign direct investment -- Rs 10 crore (~US$1.2-1.5M) within 18 months OR Rs 25 crore (~US$3-3.75M) within 36 months, plus generating employment for at least 20 resident Indians every financial year -- not on holding or extending an Employment Visa. An Employment Visa holder with no independent qualifying investment has no route into PRS. Absent PRS-level investment, an Employment Visa is a renewable-but-capped track only: extendable year-to-year by the local immigration registration office (the FRRO/FRO) up to a total of 5 years from initial issuance (confirmed at IN:employment-visa-renewability, this same file), with no further conversion after that ceiling -- a genuine structural dead end for this route, distinct from Mexico's temporary-to-permanent 4-year on-ramp (MX:temporary-resident-visa-converts-to-permanent-residency) and closer in shape to a hard wall. Trajectory read as stable: scheme unchanged since its 2016 launch, no reform proposal found this pass. Cross-corroborated across an Indian embassy source (indembastana.gov.in, reporting the MHA/PIB 2016 scheme announcement) and multiple independent aggregator/law-firm sources (expatorbit.com, mondaq.com, taxnews.ey.com, expatfocus.com) all converging on the same eligibility shape; direct fetch attempts against mha.gov.in and pib.gov.in primary PDFs (prsforeigninvestors_17042017.pdf, the PIB press release, and the MHA work-visa FAQ PDF) all returned HTTP 403 this pass -- the embassy source is the closest reachable primary-institutional citation, not a first-choice aggregator paraphrase. Closes our records (converts_to_pr was the sole remaining data_gap cause on this route).

fact_label: Tax residency — 182-day rule and RNOR-to-ROR transition
value_raw: Resident if present 182+ days/year (or 60+ days current year + 365+ days across preceding 4 years). A Resident is further RNOR (India-sourced income only) if an NR in 9 of the preceding 10 tax years, or present ≤729 days across the preceding 7 tax years — typically the first 2-3 tax years of continuous stay. Once neither RNOR condition holds, the person becomes ROR and India taxes worldwide income, including foreign-client income never remitted to India.
notes: A real, previously-undocumented income-viability constraint for anyone genuinely settling in Goa rather than tourist-visa-hopping: after roughly 2-3 consecutive years at 182+ days/year, RNOR protection lapses and worldwide income (including remote/freelance earnings from foreign clients, paid into a foreign account and never brought into India) becomes taxable in India. Not independently cross-checked against India's own Income Tax Act text or incometaxindia.gov.in this pass — PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries is a reputable professional-advisory source but a single one. Paper-vs-practice divergence: Not yet checked — no first-hand account found of enforcement against a foreign resident's undeclared foreign-client income specifically.

value_raw: India has 94 comprehensive Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) plus 8 limited-scope treaties, using credit and exemption methods to prevent double taxation of the same income; a unilateral Section 91 relief mechanism covers residents whose home country has no DTAA with India at all. Claiming relief requires filing/documentation with Indian tax authorities, not automatic.
notes: Directly relevant once a foreign national in Goa transitions from RNOR to ROR status (see IN:tax-residency-182-day-rule-and-rnor-to-ror-transition) and India begins taxing worldwide income — relief exists via treaty but is a filing obligation, not a passive exemption. Whether the reader's own home country has a DTAA with India, and its specific terms, is nationality-dependent and not surveyed here. Aggregator/law-firm-blog tier source, not independently verified against India's own Income Tax Department DTAA list (incometaxindia.gov.in) this pass.

fact_label: Individual income tax slab rates — new regime, FY2026-27
value_raw: 0% up to ₹4 lakh; 5% ₹4-8 lakh; 10% ₹8-12 lakh; 15% ₹12-16 lakh; 20% ₹16-20 lakh; 25% ₹20-24 lakh; 30% above ₹24 lakh. Section 156 of the Income Tax Act, 2025 (successor provision to Section 87A under the repealed 1961 Act) rebate zeroes tax liability up to ₹12 lakh taxable income under the new regime (₹5 lakh under the old regime).
unit: ₹ lakh/year (top marginal rate 30% above ₹24 lakh, ≈$27,000-28,500 depending on exchange rate)
notes: Slab brackets unchanged from FY2025-26 per multiple sources (bajajhousingfinance.in, cleartax.in). CORRECTED 2026-08-24 ([specialist], responding to [specialist] citation-integrity audit task): originally cited as 'Section 87A' — that is the OLD 1961 Act's numbering for this rebate, no longer current law under the new Income Tax Act, 2025 (effective FY2026-27). Re-fetched bajajhousingfinance.in directly and confirmed it actually attributes the rebate to 'Section 157,' never mentioning 87A at all — the original fact's own section number didn't even match its cited source. Further research found bajajhousingfinance.in's '157' is itself wrong: Section 157 of the new Act covers relief for salary received in arrears/advance, an unrelated provision (confirmed via CAclubindia's 'Section 87A and Section 156 Rebate Explained: Why Tax May Still Be Payable Below Rs 12 Lakh,' which explicitly distinguishes Section 156 from Section 157). The correct section is 156, confirmed via strong cross-corroboration across independent tax-advisory sources: ClearTax ('Section 156 Income Tax Act 2025-Tax Rebate Explained'), Axis Max Life, ICICI Prudential Life, TaxGuru, Godrej Capital, eztax.in ('Section-156: Rebate of income-tax in case of certain individuals'), AUBSP ('Income Tax (No. 2) Act 2025: Section 156'), and TaxTMI's direct comparison piece 'Clause 156 of the Income Tax Bill, 2025 Vs Section 87A of the Income Tax Act, 1961.' Section 156 has three sub-sections: (1) old-regime rebate, 100% of tax or ₹12,500 whichever is less, income ≤₹5 lakh; (2) new-regime rebate, 100% of tax or ₹60,000 whichever is less, income ≤₹12 lakh (per eztax.in's quoted provision text), with marginal relief above ₹12 lakh; (3) caps the sub-section-2 deduction at the tax payable under Section 202(1)'s rate schedule. A search-indexed incometaxindia.gov.in page is titled 'Section 156 - Income Tax,' consistent with this — but direct fetch of incometaxindia.gov.in returned 403 (bot-blocked) both attempts, so this was not read against the government's own primary text directly this pass; treat as cross-corroborated across independent secondary tax-advisory sources, not primary-institutional-confirmed. Given the wrong candidate (157) was independently disproven and 156 converges across ~8 unrelated advisory sites, confidence raised to High for the section-number correction itself; the underlying slab-rate figures were already correct and unchanged from the prior pass.
